provenance.method: lesson notes written from the NERDC 2025 scheme of work outline; every week keeps its scheme topic and bullets as the teaching spine

topics.title: Revision of sss two work
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to recall basic ledger entries.
The students should be able to complete a short quiz on SSS 2 accounting topics.

Introduction:
Today we will revise what we learned in SSS 2 to refresh our memory.
This revision will help us build a strong foundation for this term's work.

Content:
We will start with a warm-up exercise on ledger accounts.
Students will practice posting entries to the ledger from source documents.
We will then have a quiz covering key topics from last year including:
- Double entry system
- Final accounts preparation
- Bank reconciliation statements
- Control accounts

Class activity:
Students will work in pairs to complete a set of ledger postings.
Each pair will exchange their work with another pair for marking and correction.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is the purpose of a ledger account?
2. List the three main types of ledger accounts.
3. Explain the double entry system in your own words.

Summary:
Today's revision has refreshed our knowledge of basic accounting principles from SSS 2.
This foundation will help us understand more complex topics this term.

topics.title: Accounting concepts
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to state the main accounting principles and conventions.
The students should be able to explain how accounting concepts affect financial reporting.

Introduction:
We have revised the basics of accounting and now we will study the concepts that guide accounting practice.
These concepts are fundamental to understanding how financial statements are prepared.

Content:
Accounting concepts are the basic rules and assumptions that guide accounting practice.
Key principles include:
- Going concern assumption: Business will continue operating indefinitely
- Accruals: Revenue and expenses are recorded when earned/incurred
- Consistency: Same accounting methods used year after year
- Prudence: Recognize losses immediately but profits only certain
- Materiality: Only significant items need detailed accounting treatment

Class activity:
Students will analyze a case study of a small business (like a local market stall) and identify which accounting concepts apply to different transactions.

Evaluation questions:
1. List four accounting principles and explain each briefly.
2. How does the prudence concept affect inventory valuation?
3. Why is consistency important in financial reporting?
4. A business buys a new generator for N50,000. Which concept determines how this is recorded?

Summary:
Accounting concepts provide the framework for preparing financial statements and ensuring consistency in reporting.

topics.title: Books of original entry
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify different types of journals and day books.
The students should be able to record transactions in the appropriate books of original entry.

Introduction:
Last week we studied the concepts that guide accounting practice.
This week we will learn about the first books where transactions are recorded before posting to the ledger.

Content:
The books of original entry are where transactions are first recorded chronologically.
Types include:
- Sales journal: For all credit sales to customers
- Purchases journal: For all credit purchases from suppliers
- Returns journal: For goods returned by customers or to suppliers
- Cash book: For all cash transactions (received and paid)
- General journal: For unique transactions that don't fit other books

For example, when Alhaji Umar buys goods on credit from Iya Bose market stall, this would be recorded in the purchases journal.

Class activity:
Students will work in groups to record a series of transactions in the appropriate books of original entry.
Transactions will include sales, purchases, returns, and cash payments.

Evaluation questions:
1. Name three types of books of original entry.
2. Where would you record a credit sale of goods?
3. What is the purpose of the general journal?
4. A business pays N5,000 cash for kerosene for their generator. Which book would this be recorded in?

Summary:
The books of original entry serve as the first point of recording transactions and are essential for maintaining proper accounting records.

topics.title: Ledger accounts
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain the rules for posting to ledger accounts.
The students should be able to post transactions from books of original entry to ledger accounts.

Introduction:
Last week we learned about recording transactions in books of original entry.
This week we will learn how to transfer these records to ledger accounts.

Content:
Ledger accounts are the main books of account where transactions are classified by type.
Posting rules include:
- Debit the receiver, credit the giver
- Personal accounts: Debit the receiver, credit the giver
- Real accounts: Debit what comes in, credit what goes out
- Nominal accounts: Debit all expenses and losses, credit all incomes and gains

For example, when a business sells goods on credit to Alhaji Umar, we debit Alhaji Umar's account (personal) and credit the sales account (nominal).

Class activity:
Students will practice posting from various books of original entry to appropriate ledger accounts.
Each student will complete a set of postings and exchange with a partner for verification.

Evaluation questions:
1. State the three golden rules of accounting.
2. What is the difference between a personal and nominal account?
3. How do you post a credit purchase of goods?
4. A business pays N10,000 rent for their shop. How is this posted to the ledger?

Summary:
Ledger accounts organize transactions by type and follow specific posting rules to maintain the double entry system.

topics.title: Trial balance
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to extract a trial balance from ledger accounts.
The students should be able to identify and correct common errors in trial balance preparation.

Introduction:
Last week we learned how to post transactions to ledger accounts.
This week we will learn how to prepare a trial balance to check the accuracy of our postings.

Content:
A trial balance is a statement listing all ledger accounts with their debit or credit balances.
It is prepared to verify that total debits equal total credits.
Steps to prepare:
1. Extract balances from all ledger accounts
2. List accounts with their balances in debit or credit columns
3. Total both columns
4. Check if totals agree

If totals don't agree, common errors include:
- Posting to wrong side of account
- Omission of an account
- Error in totaling
- Transposition error (e.g., writing 1200 instead of 1020)

Class activity:
Students will work in pairs to extract a trial balance from a given set of ledger accounts.
They will then identify and correct any errors in the trial balance.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is the purpose of preparing a trial balance?
2. List three errors that would not be revealed by a trial balance.
3. A trial balance shows total debits of N500,000 and total credits of N495,000. What is the likely error?
4. How would you treat an account with a nil balance in a trial balance?

Summary:
The trial balance is an important step in the accounting cycle to verify the equality of debits and credits before preparing final accounts.

topics.title: Trading, profit and loss
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to prepare a trading account to calculate gross profit.
The students should be able to prepare a profit and loss account to calculate net profit.

Introduction:
Last week we learned how to prepare a trial balance to check our accounting records.
This week we will learn how to use these records to prepare trading and profit and loss accounts.

Content:
The trading account shows buying and selling activities to calculate gross profit.
Opening inventory + Purchases - Closing inventory = Cost of goods sold
Sales - Cost of goods sold = Gross profit

The profit and loss account shows all other income and expenses to calculate net profit.
Gross profit + Other income - Expenses = Net profit

For example, a business that sells danfo spare parts would show all spare part purchases and sales in the trading account, while expenses like rent and wages appear in the profit and loss account.

Class activity:
Students will prepare complete trading and profit and loss accounts from a trial balance and additional information.
They will calculate both gross and net profit for a hypothetical business.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is the difference between gross profit and net profit?
2. List three items that would appear in a trading account.
3. How is closing inventory treated in the trading account?
4. A business has sales of N1,000,000, purchases of N600,000 and opening inventory of N100,000. If closing inventory is N150,000, calculate gross profit.

Summary:
The trading and profit and loss accounts summarize a business's trading activities and profitability over a period.

topics.title: Balance sheet
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to prepare a balance sheet from given information.
The students should be able to differentiate between assets and liabilities.

Introduction:
Last week we learned how to prepare trading and profit and loss accounts.
This week we will learn how to prepare a balance sheet, which shows the financial position of a business.

Content:
A balance sheet shows what a business owns (assets) and owes (liabilities) at a specific date.
Assets are resources owned by the business with future economic benefit.
- Current assets: Cash, inventory, receivables (convertible to cash within a year)
- Fixed assets: Land, buildings, equipment (used in operations for longer than a year)

Liabilities are obligations of the business to outsiders.
- Current liabilities: Payables, short-term loans (due within a year)
- Long-term liabilities: Loans due after more than a year

The accounting equation is: Assets = Liabilities + Capital

For example, a small business that sells plantain chips would show fryers as fixed assets and money owed to suppliers as current liabilities.

Class activity:
Students will prepare a balance sheet for a hypothetical business using information from previous accounts prepared.
They will classify items correctly as assets or liabilities.

Evaluation questions:
1. Differentiate between current assets and fixed assets.
2. List three examples of current liabilities.
3. Explain the accounting equation.
4. A business has assets of N2,000,000 and liabilities of N800,000. What is the capital?

Summary:
The balance sheet provides a snapshot of a business's financial position at a specific date, showing what it owns and owes.

topics.title: Adjustments: accruals
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify and record accruals and prepayments.
The students should be able to adjust accounts for accruals and prepayments.

Introduction:
Last week we learned how to prepare a balance sheet showing a business's financial position.
This week we will learn how to make adjustments for accruals and prepayments to ensure accounts are accurate.

Content:
Accruals and prepayments are adjustments needed to match expenses with the period they relate to.

Accruals (expenses owing but not yet paid):
- Expenses incurred but not yet paid
- Added to expenses in profit and loss account
- Shown as current liabilities in balance sheet

Prepayments (expenses paid in advance):
- Expenses paid before they are incurred
- Deducted from expenses in profit and loss account
- Shown as current assets in balance sheet

For example, if a business pays N12,000 rent annually in January, by December, N11,000 would be expense and N1,000 would be prepayment (current asset).

Class activity:
Students will work in groups to identify accruals and prepayments in a case study and make the necessary adjustments to accounts.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is an accrual and how is it treated in final accounts?
2. Explain how a prepayment is different from an accrual.
3. A business pays N60,000 insurance on January 1 for the year. By June 30, what amount would be expense and what amount prepayment?
4. Why are accruals and prepayments necessary in accrual accounting?

Summary:
Accruals and prepayments ensure that expenses are matched to the period they relate to, providing a more accurate picture of profitability.

topics.title: Depreciation
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to calculate depreciation using straight line and reducing balance methods.
The students should be able to account for depreciation in final accounts.

Introduction:
Last week we learned about adjustments for accruals and prepayments.
This week we will learn about depreciation, another important adjustment for fixed assets.

Content:
Depreciation is the systematic allocation of the cost of a fixed asset over its useful life.

Straight line method:
- Depreciation is constant each year
- Calculation: (Cost - Residual value) ÷ Useful life

Reducing balance method:
- Depreciation decreases each year
- Calculation: Cost × Depreciation rate

For example, a generator costing N100,000 with a 5-year life and no residual value would have annual depreciation of N20,000 straight line, or N20,000 in first year, N16,000 in second year (20% reducing balance).

Depreciation appears in profit and loss account as expense and is accumulated in balance sheet as deduction from fixed asset cost.

Class activity:
Students will calculate depreciation for various assets using both methods and record the entries in accounts.
They will then prepare extracts of financial statements showing depreciation.

Evaluation questions:
1. Explain the difference between straight line and reducing balance depreciation.
2. A delivery van costs N1,500,000 with a 4-year life and no residual value. Calculate depreciation for each year using straight line method.
3. How is depreciation treated in final accounts?
4. Why is depreciation necessary in accounting?

Summary:
Depreciation recognizes that fixed assets lose value over time and allocates this cost systematically to the periods benefiting from the asset.

topics.title: Revision and WAEC practice
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to complete a WAEC past paper question paper one.
The students should be able to identify common question patterns in WAEC accounting exams.

Introduction:
This is our final week of term and we will revise all topics covered and practice WAEC exam questions.
This will help you prepare for your final examinations.

Content:
We will work through a complete WAEC past paper question paper one.
The paper will cover all topics studied this term:
- Accounting concepts
- Books of original entry
- Ledger accounts
- Trial balance
- Trading, profit and loss accounts
- Balance sheet
- Adjustments (accruals, depreciation)

We will discuss common question patterns and effective exam techniques.

Class activity:
Students will work individually to complete the past paper within the time limit.
After completion, we will mark and correct the paper together, discussing any areas of difficulty.

Evaluation questions:
1. Which accounting concept requires expenses to be recorded when incurred rather than when paid?
2. How would you record a return of goods to a supplier?
3. What is the purpose of a trial balance?
4. A business has sales of N2,000,000, cost of goods sold of N1,200,000 and expenses of N400,000. Calculate net profit.
5. Explain the difference between a fixed asset and a current asset.

Summary:
Today's revision has covered all key topics and practiced exam techniques to prepare you for your final examinations.
